note:
Vol. II No. 9. The masthead is dated 17 June and the interior editorial block visibly prints 10 June; corpus.json records the printed mismatch and so does this reading. A photographer's hand covers part of source page 25.

THIS IS THE SANITARY ISSUE. The editor's second and far angrier complaint about the state of the streets is answered inside the same paper by a town meeting held at the Presbyterian church, whose resolutions are set cleanly and in full — the best-transcribed civic document in the whole reading range, with a chairman, a secretary, four speakers and a committee of seven all named. Around it: the first annual fair of the Episcopal ladies at Bates' new auction room, a school district meeting called to build a school house, green peas from up the North Branch, and Hubbard & Co. selling forty thousand feet of hewn building timber.

claims.notes:
THE TOWN'S SURFACE, TWO WEEKS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE, DESCRIBED BY SOMEBODY WALKING IT AND FURIOUS. Four facts and every one of them is about the ground the reconstruction models.

1. THE STREETS ARE FOUL — 'would disgrace a piggery'. 2. THE VACANT LOTS AND THE SPACES BETWEEN BUILDINGS HOLD STANDING WATER: 'holes filled with green putrid water and decaying vegetable matter'. That is the same complaint as 1835-05-20's 'sunken spots in the vacant lots all about the buildings', four weeks later and worse, and it is the best-evidenced statement in this corpus about what the unbuilt ground BETWEEN Chicago's buildings actually looked like in the summer of 1835: not lawn, not bare earth, but pitted, water-filled and rank. 3. BARRELS OF PUTRID MEAT IN A BUILDING IN THE MOST POPULOUS QUARTER — reported at second hand ('We learn that') and quoted as such. 4. THE PUBLIC HOUSES ARE OVERFULL and strangers are sleeping on floors, which is the same crowd the flour price and the land sale describe from other angles.

THE TOWN IS STILL WELL. 'Our town still continues healthy' — and 1835-06-24 says so again in the middle of a state-wide cholera scare. So the conditions described here had NOT produced an epidemic by the scene date, which matters because it would be easy to read this paragraph as describing a sick town. It describes a filthy healthy one whose editor expects that not to last.

AND IT WAS ACTED ON, THE SAME WEEK. The closing lines were set after the town meeting had been held; the meeting's own resolutions are the next claim. The column is interleaved with three others line by line and `lines_of_claim` names only this article's lines.

claims.quote:
TOWN MEETING.
Pursuant to previous public notice, a public meeting of the citizens of Chicago was held at the Presbyterian church yesterday morning. The meeting was called to order by Col. G. S. Hubbard, and E. K. Hubbard was chosen Chairman, and J. Curtiss was chosen Secretary.
The object of the meeting was stated by Col. G. S. Hubbard, and pertinent addresses were severally made by Messrs. Peck, Morris, Fullerton, and others; and on motion the following resolutions were unanimously adopted:
Resolved, That the situation of this town, abounding in nuisances, is such as to require immediate and energetic action on the part of its officers—that it is only by such action that our present state of health and prosperity can be preserved.
Resolved, That the present Trustees be requested to exercise the necessary powers to cleanse and purify the streets of the town, and to do whatever may be necessary for them to do to preserve the health of the citizens; and that they be directed to obtain the requisite funds on the faith of the town, or in any other way which may be feasible.
Resolved, That we will sustain the present Trustees in prompt and efficient action upon this subject.
Resolved, That if the Trustees find the same necessary, they be requested to call another public meeting of the citizens, to act upon this subject, and to take any powers which may be necessary and which they may be found not to have.
Resolved, That there be a committee of seven persons appointed to co-operate with the Trustees in effecting the objects of this meeting; and Messrs. J. Curtiss, Peck, B. S. Morris, A. N. Fullerton, A. Sweet, J. T. Temple, and B. King were chosen said committee.
E. K. HUBBARD, Ch'n.
J. CURTISS, Sec'y.

claims.notes:
THE TOWN GOVERNS ITSELF IN A CHURCH, AND THE CHURCH IS THE PRESBYTERIAN. A public meeting of the CITIZENS OF CHICAGO, held in the Presbyterian church on the morning of 16 June 1835 — a building already documented in this corpus (T-0310 read its dedication in January 1834) now shown in civic use two weeks before the scene date. The same building hosts School District No. 4's meeting on 7 July (next claim but one). A meeting house doing double duty as the town's assembly room is a fact about how this town used its few large interiors, and it belongs beside the Exchange Coffee House and Bates' auction room, which did the same job.

THE RESOLUTIONS ARE A CONSTITUTIONAL DOCUMENT AS MUCH AS A SANITARY ONE. They ask the PRESENT Trustees to act — the board whose replacement election kept being adjourned for want of a copy of the new charter — direct them to borrow 'on the faith of the town' to pay for it, and offer, if the Trustees 'may be found not to have' the powers, to call another meeting to give them some. That is a town whose citizens are working around a legal vacuum they know they are in.

NINE MEN NAMED, AND SEVEN OF THEM ON ONE COMMITTEE. Four of the nine are placed by their own advertising elsewhere in these eight issues: J. Curtiss (South Water Street, first door west of Jones, King & Co.), J. T. Temple (two stores and a dwelling to let), B. King (Byram King of Jones, King & Co., read as such on the warrant of the School District notice in this same issue, which signs 'BYRAM KING, Clerk'), and E. K. Hubbard (lots in the School Section, agent for the Rezigue house). Peck, Morris, Fullerton and Sweet are minted on this claim alone. Col. G. S. Hubbard and E. K. Hubbard are NOT merged with each other or with Hubbard & Co.; that is T-0299's work.

This is the cleanest-set column of the eight issues — the transcriber gives it as continuous prose with no losses — which is why the quote runs to full sentences where most claims here are read through breakage.

claims.normalized: The examination of claims under the Chicago Treaty of 1833, by the commissioner on behalf of the U. States, will be commenced on the 29th instant.
claims.notes:
THE 1833 TREATY CLAIMS COMMISSION SITS IN CHICAGO ON 29 JUNE 1835 — two days before the scene date. Whatever room it used was in use at the modelled moment, and the town would have been holding the claimants. The Treaty of Chicago of 1833 is the instrument by which the Potawatomi ceded the land the town stands on, and its claims process was still running two years later, in the town, in the same fortnight as the federal land sale. Nothing here places the commission or names the commissioner, and neither is invented.

The 'payment last fall' which the standing Pocket Book Found notice refers to — a pocket book 'found by an Indian in Chicago during the payment last fall' — is the annuity payment under the same treaty, so this issue and that one are the same business a year apart.

claims.notes:
GREEN PEAS, RAISED UP THE NORTH BRANCH, SOLD IN CHICAGO ON 16 JUNE 1835. Small and unusually useful: it dates a garden crop to the middle of June in this latitude in this year, and it locates market gardening UP THE NORTH BRANCH — not on the platted blocks and not on the open prairie, but along the north fork of the river. It is the only statement in these eight issues about where the town's fresh food was grown, and it is printed as a novelty, which suggests the traffic was new.

The prices current in the same issues quote no vegetables except potatoes and beans, and beans read 'none' every week, so a pea crop coming in is genuinely news.

claims.notes:
TWO BUILDINGS AND AN INSTITUTION IN ONE NOTICE. BATES' NEW AUCTION ROOM is named — which is what supplies the possessive missing from the 1835-06-10 land-auction advertisement's 'Auction Room, Dearborn Street' — and it is NEW, and it is big enough and public enough to hold an evening fair as well as a two-day land sale. That is the only Chicago interior in these eight issues described by two different uses.

THE PROTESTANT EPISCOPAL CHURCH OF THIS TOWN HAS A LADIES' SOCIETY, and it is holding its FIRST ANNUAL fair. The congregation therefore exists as an organised body by June 1835 — this corpus has the Presbyterian and Baptist meeting houses as buildings and now has a third denomination as a body, though NOT as a building: nothing here says the Episcopalians had one, and the fact that they borrowed an auction room rather than using their own church is weak evidence that they did not.

'A FAIR BEING A NOVELTY IN CHICAGO' and 'breaking in upon the monotonous cry of Land sales and land speculations' are the two phrases to keep: the first dates the town's first bazaar to 18 June 1835, thirteen days before the scene date, and the second is how the fortnight before the land sale felt to the people living through it.

SCHOOL DISTRICT NO. 4 HAS NO SCHOOL HOUSE ON THE SCENE DATE AND IS ABOUT TO MEET ABOUT BUILDING ONE — the meeting is called for 7 July 1835, six days AFTER the modelled day. So on 1 July the district exists, has a clerk, and has no building; anything the reconstruction puts up for it would be wrong. That is a negative fact and it is worth as much as a positive one.

THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH AGAIN, and this is its second civic use in one issue (the town meeting of 16 June is the other). A district without a school house meets in the meeting-house, which is what a town with three large interiors does.

SCHOOL DISTRICT No. 4, not No. 2 — T-0310 read School District No. 2's trustee election held in the Baptist meeting house in January 1834. Two numbered districts, eighteen months apart, meeting in two different churches. Byram King the district clerk is read as the Byram King of Jones, King & Co. on the strength of the unusual forename and the same town in the same month; the merge is stated here rather than performed silently, and if it is wrong the two men separate cleanly.

claims.notes:
THE PLACEMENT CONFLICT, PRINTED. Five days earlier the same firm advertised its New Store 'in La Salle street, a few doors South of Hubbard & Co's. brick store'; here the same store is 'next door to Messrs. Harmon, Loomis & Co.', and Harmon, Loomis & Co. state their own store to be IN SOUTH WATER STREET. Both notices are signed by the same firm, both describe the same building ('the store of the subscribers'), and they name two different streets' neighbours.

WHAT IS NOT DONE ABOUT IT. Neither reading is discarded and neither street is declared wrong. Three explanations fit and the paper chooses none: a CORNER LOT at La Salle and South Water would make both true at once; 'next door' may be loose for 'near'; or the firm moved inside five days, which the 'To Let' notice makes unlikely since it is letting rooms over the store it has just taken. `business.street` keeps La Salle Street because that is the firm's own explicit street in its own opening advertisement, and this claim's anchor keeps Harmon, Loomis & Co. because that is what THIS notice says. A pass that can test it — T-0324's shape of problem, two addresses for one advertiser in one paper — should take it.

THE DATELINE PRINTS '1833' and cannot stand: the firm opened on 11 June 1835 and this is its second notice. Read as 1835-06-16.

WHAT IS CERTAIN EITHER WAY: their store had a second storey with rooms over it, offered to let two weeks before the scene date.

PETER COHEN IS STILL AT HIS OLD STAND ON 11 JUNE 1835, WHICH IS THE POINT. T-0257's worked fixture read Cohen's standing advertisement of 3 November 1834 — 'at his store [be]low Messrs. Newberry and Dole's on south water street' — and this pass now has him opening a NEW stock at that SAME stand three weeks before the scene date. Ruling 3 gives a documented business survival unless contradicted; this is better than that, it is positive continuity, and it means the storefront the fixture placed is occupied and trading on 1 July 1835 without any liberty being required.

THE PLACEMENT IS INHERITED AND SAYS SO. 'AT HIS OLD STAND' names no street and no anchor; the offset text quoted in the placement is that phrase, and the bracketed part of the normalized offset is the 1834 advertisement's own words, attributed. This claim does not re-place Cohen — it carries the fixture's placement forward on the warrant of his own words.

AND IT ANCHORS A THIRD PARTY. L. W. Montgomery's boot and shoe shop is 'next door to P. Cohen's Store', so Montgomery's placement depends on Cohen still standing here, which this notice supplies.

claims.notes:
FORTY THOUSAND FEET OF HEWN TIMBER, SUITABLE FOR BUILDING, ON SALE IN CHICAGO TWO WEEKS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. 'M.' is the Roman thousand, as it is throughout this paper's advertising ('per 1000' in the prices current). HEWN, not sawn — squared with an axe or broadaxe, which is the timber of a braced frame and a log structure rather than of a balloon frame, and it is offered as a commodity by a dry-goods house alongside sperm oil and hams.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE PRICE TABLE. The prices current quotes 'Square timber, length ft 5 a 6' every week, which says squared timber was a traded good; this says HOW MUCH of it was standing in one merchant's yard at once. Forty thousand feet is a large stack — enough framing for a good many buildings — and it is a visible object somewhere in the town in June 1835. Nothing places it, and the yard is not invented.

Hubbard & Co's own store is the brick one in La Salle Street (per Magie & Wilkinson); the timber's location is not stated.

A land-seller receiving callers at a Lake Street house and a physician keeping his rooms in it make it a working commercial building and not just an inn, two weeks before the scene date.

Offered nine days before the federal land sale, by a private holder, which is the speculative market running alongside the government one.

claims.notes:
A WALK ACROSS TOWN, DESCRIBED BY ITS TWO ENDS: Mulford's store and Col. Owen's house. Neither is placed anywhere in this corpus, so the line cannot be drawn — but it names a PRIVATE DWELLING by its owner as a landmark somebody could be expected to find, which is what a well-known house does, and Col. T. J. V. Owen is the man who called the April 1835 Democratic meeting to order and sat on its resolutions committee. A named house belonging to a named public figure is a target the page images or a later issue could locate, and it is worth recording as a wanted position rather than losing.

A SILVER CANDLESTICK, and the top or slide off it. Small domestic metalwork, in a town where the paper is advertising for a coppersmith. J. H. Mulford also runs the 'Twig This' dunning notice ('pay up by the 1st of June, or they will be sued without further notice—fair warning'), which is the same man's store in the same weeks and is not separately claimed.

claims.notes: THE LAST MARINE LIST BEFORE THE LAND SALE, and it is short — four entries for 14 and 15 June against seventeen the week before. A second STEAM BOAT, the Jefferson from Buffalo, and the Llewellyn and the Swan on their St. Joseph shuttle again. The rest of the list is lost to the interleave: the column runs into the Chicago Lands advertisement line by line and only these four survive as readable entries, so NO WEEKLY TOTAL is asserted from it. The one master whose name will not resolve, on the Semiramis, is left bracketed rather than guessed.
